What Would Happen to You if Earth's Poles Flipped?

Episode 104 of a daily journey through the universe. 🧲
We look at Earth's magnetic field: the invisible shield made by our molten iron core, magnetic poles that have swapped hundreds of times, the last full flip about 780,000 years ago, the Laschamp event 41,000 years ago, and the growing South Atlantic Anomaly.

segments.text: What if your compass suddenly pointed south? It's happened hundreds of times.
Deep inside Earth, molten iron swirls around the core. That motion creates a giant magnetic field around our planet.
segments.headline: A magnet made of molten iron

segments.text: That invisible shield deflects charged particles from the Sun. When some sneak in near the poles, we see auroras.
segments.headline: Our invisible shield

segments.text: But the field isn't permanent. Every so often, magnetic north and south swap places.
segments.headline: North and south swap

segments.text: We know because volcanic rocks freeze the direction of the field when they cool. The seafloor is striped with flips.
segments.headline: Recorded in rock

segments.text: The last full flip happened about seven hundred and eighty thousand years ago.
And about forty-one thousand years ago, the field nearly collapsed for a few centuries. That's called the Laschamp event.
Today, a weak spot over the South Atlantic is growing. Satellites passing over it get more radiation glitches.
segments.headline: A growing weak spot

segments.text: Is a flip coming? Nobody knows. And a flip takes thousands of years, so no compass emergency tomorrow.
segments.headline: Is a flip coming?
